title: Education To Script or Not to Script Elana
author: Elana
summary: A special education reading teacher named Elana shares a perspective shift on scripted direct instruction curricula: after initial resistance, she found that well-designed scripts actually freed her professional judgment rather than constraining it. Working with both EBLI and Reading Mastery, Elana discovered that scripts freed her cognitive resources from low-stakes micro-decisions -- what words to use, what text to select, how to phrase an error correction -- and redirected them toward what actually requires expert judgment: reading student cues, adjusting delivery pacing, and responding to the dynamic state of the class. The article is a practitioner's rebuttal to the common assumption that professional autonomy in teaching is best expressed through curriculum design rather than instructional delivery.
points: The teacher autonomy argument against scripted curricula conflates two forms of professional judgment: curriculum design and instructional delivery -- well-designed scripts enhance the latter by offloading the former, freeing expert attention for the non-routine elements that require genuine responsiveness.

Scripts designed with cognitive science principles build in linguistic precision that evidence-based instruction requires -- exact word choice for error corrections, consistent framing of phonological concepts -- precision improvised teaching rarely achieves consistently.

Elana's experience aligns with cognitive load research: expert performance in complex domains improves when practitioners are freed from routine sub-decisions and can allocate full attention to the non-routine elements requiring genuine expertise.

Adopting a scripted curriculum does not signal lack of trust in teachers; it signals recognition that professional expertise should be directed toward student responsiveness, not repeated from-scratch curriculum design.

Resistance to scripted curricula often reflects a conflation of professional identity with creative input into materials -- once teachers experience the cognitive freedom good scripts enable, that resistance typically decreases.
quotes: When I first heard of scripted lessons, I used to shudder. I couldn't stand the idea of not using all the knowledge I had just acquired around the Science of Reading and planning my own lessons. I wanted to lead those lessons, but I mistakenly believed scripted lessons limited my decision-making power.
